title: Fluids
summary: Fluids exert pressure that grows with depth ($P=P_0+\rho gh$). Buoyancy equals the weight of displaced fluid (Archimedes). Pascal's principle powers hydraulics, continuity conserves flow rate, and Bernoulli links pressure to speed.

buoyant force.plain: Upward force on a submerged object.

concept_sections.heading: Pressure and depth
concept_sections.explanation: Pressure rises with depth: $P=P_0+\rho gh$, and acts equally in all directions at a point.

concept_sections.heading: Buoyancy
concept_sections.explanation: A submerged object feels an upward force equal to the weight of displaced fluid: $F_b=\rho_{fluid}Vg$. It floats if that matches its weight.

concept_sections.heading: Pascal's principle
concept_sections.explanation: Pressure applied to a confined fluid transmits everywhere, so a hydraulic system multiplies force by the piston-area ratio.

concept_sections.heading: Continuity
concept_sections.explanation: Incompressible flow keeps $Av$ constant, so a narrower pipe speeds the fluid up.

concept_sections.heading: Bernoulli's principle
concept_sections.explanation: Along a streamline, higher speed means lower pressure ($P+\tfrac12\rho v^2+\rho gh$ constant) — the idea behind lift and atomizers.

real_world_examples.title: Floating and sinking
real_world_examples.scenario: A cork floats; a coin sinks.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Objects float when their density is below the fluid's — a buoyancy comparison.

real_world_examples.title: Hydraulic brakes
real_world_examples.scenario: A light pedal press stops a car.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Pascal's principle amplifies the force through the brake fluid.

real_world_examples.title: A shower curtain pulling in
real_world_examples.scenario: The curtain billows toward the water.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Fast-moving air lowers pressure (Bernoulli), so outside air pushes it in.
